title: Scalar history criteria for the first loss of full sliding under variable fluid injection
shortTitle: The injection point decides when a fault stops sliding forward
oneLine: In the standard circular model of injection-driven slow slip, the slip rate at the injection point decides when the whole fault first stops sliding forward: under stated conditions the centre stops first, almost any abrupt cut ends full sliding, and for a point source no linear taper can halve the rate.
abstract: Fluid injected into a fault can drive slow, aseismic slip that spreads as an expanding crack. When the injection rate is reduced, part of the fault eventually stops slipping forward, and crack-based size and volume laws cease to apply. This candidate asks when this first happens, in the standard circular model with constant friction, zero fracture energy and zero Poisson ratio, and shows that one scalar quantity, the slip-rate history at the injection point, decides it. For a point source, a Gaussian source or any positive mixture of Gaussian widths and any injection rate that rises and then falls, the whole slipping disk moves forward exactly when the injection point does. For piecewise-smooth rates with any number of rises, falls and steps, the same holds over an interval exactly when the injection-point history has stayed nonnegative throughout it, under stated startup conditions; the crack radius then exists and grows automatically, and full sliding is lost first at the injection point. Explicit consequences include an abrupt-drop tolerance of roughly the square root of source width over stage duration (about 10⁻³ at wellbore scale), a two-term finite-radius criterion with a rigorous remainder, a closed-form deadline after shut-in by which full sliding must have ended, and, for a point source, the result that no linear taper can halve the rate without loss of full sliding. Annular sources can violate the centre-first property. The results concern the first loss of full sliding only, not the later slip pulse or seismic hazard. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

keyResults: Instantaneous criterion (Theorem 1, Proposition 3.3, proof): for a point source, a Gaussian source or any positive Gaussian mixture and a rate that rises then falls, the slip rate is nonnegative throughout the disk at a given time if and only if it is nonnegative at the injection point.

Historical criteria (Theorems A, B, G and Proposition 4.1, proof): for piecewise-smooth or stepped rates with any number of rises and falls, under stated startup conditions, full sliding holds over an interval exactly when the centre history has stayed nonnegative; the crack radius exists and grows automatically, full sliding is lost first at the centre, and for a point source any downward jump ends it at once.

Abrupt drops (equation 26, proof): after a constant-rate stage of duration T with a Gaussian source, the largest tolerated relative drop is below √(ε/(T+ε)), about 10⁻³ at wellbore scale for illustrative parameters.
Inner limit (Theorem 3, proof): in the critically stressed limit the slip rate at radius r is the centre slip rate delayed by a random diffusive first-passage time.
Finite radius (Propositions 7.2 and 7.3, proof with numerically verified constants): a uniform error bound and a two-term centre criterion A*Hq(t) − (2α/R)q(t−) with a rigorous remainder.

Schedules (Proposition 8.2 and Corollary 8.4, proof): after shut-in no crack survives beyond t_s + f c_p V/τ_d − ε, so full sliding ends before then; for a point source no linear taper can halve the rate, the inner-limit threshold being ½√(L/(T+L)) and the finite-radius one strictly smaller.

narration: When does a fault stop sliding forward everywhere? An Evidence Press briefing. Pumping fluid into rock along a fault can make the fault slip slowly, without an earthquake. In the simplest models the slipping patch grows as an expanding circle around the well, and every point in it slides forward. When the injection rate is turned down, the pressure near the well falls first, and at some moment part of the fault can no longer keep sliding forward. After that, rules of thumb based on an expanding crack no longer apply. This release shows that one number decides when that moment comes: the slip rate at the injection point, the centre of the patch. If the injection rate rises and then falls, the whole patch is sliding forward exactly when the centre is. For schedules with many rises, falls and steps, provided injection starts gently, the whole patch keeps sliding forward exactly as long as the centre does, so the centre is always the first place to stop. Practical consequences follow. With realistic well sizes, almost any sudden cut, of more than about a tenth of a per cent, ends full sliding at once. After shut-in there is an explicit deadline by which it must end. And for a point source, no gradual linear reduction can halve the rate without it ending. The results have written proofs and numerical checks, in an idealised model with constant friction, and they say nothing about earthquake hazard after the first stop. This is an anonymous, AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate, not peer reviewed or independently reproduced. Published on 31 October 2026, its paper and evidence are linked from the Evidence Press release page. This briefing uses an AI-generated voice and is not additional scientific evidence.

decisionObject.description: For the circular constant-friction model of injection-driven aseismic slip with a point or Gaussian source, nonnegativity of the injection-point slip-rate history is equivalent to full sliding, under stated startup conditions; full sliding is first lost at the centre; explicit drop, shut-in and taper consequences.
decisionObject.scope: Zero Poisson ratio, constant friction, zero fracture energy, homogeneous permeable layer, one-way coupling; first loss of full sliding only. Annular sources, nonzero Poisson ratio and the post-locking slip pulse are not covered.
